readerTitle: The pizzeria across the street just cut prices 30%. What do you do?
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (동네 피자 가게의 3개월) · 모든 수치는 설명용 · 소프트웨어 적용은 softwareNote로 보완
insight: 경쟁사의 가격 인하는 즉시 따라갈 일이 아니라 상대의 이유를 읽고, 좁게 막고, 약속을 보이게 하고, 평화에는 평화로 답하는 여러 판의 게임이다.
misconception: 경쟁사가 가격을 내리면 고객을 잃기 전에 바로 같은 폭으로, 또는 더 크게 내려야 한다.

sources.text: 게임이론의 표준 개념 (죄수의 딜레마, 신뢰할 수 있는 약속, 반복 게임)
Salop, S. (1986). Practices that (credibly) facilitate oligopoly co-ordination. 가격 매칭 약속이 경쟁사의 가격 인하 동기를 줄인다는 논의

factChecks.note: 계산 확인: 정가 $15 − 피자당 비용 $5 = $10. 30% 인하가 $10.50 − $5 = $5.50. 주 600판 기준 $6,000 → $3,300 (주 $2,700 감소). 같은 이익을 내려면 6,000 ÷ 5.50 = 1,091판, 약 82% 증가. 할인가에서 카드 수수료가 조금 줄지만 단순화를 위해 피자당 비용을 $5로 고정했습니다.
잃은 주문: 600판의 10% = 60판 × $10 = 주 $600. 전면 대응 비용(주 $2,700)과 비교한 수치입니다.
가격 매칭 약속이 경쟁사의 인하 동기를 줄인다는 주장은 Salop(1986) 등 산업조직론 문헌의 일반적 논의입니다. 카드에는 원리만 적었고 특정 연구 결과나 수치는 인용하지 않았습니다. 게시 전 표현을 확인하세요.
경쟁사와 가격을 합의하는 것은 대부분의 국가에서 불법(담합)이라는 일반적 경고만 적었습니다. 특정 국가의 법률 조언은 하지 않습니다.

cards.title: The pizzeria across the street just cut prices 30%.
body: Monday morning. You run a neighborhood pizzeria. Across the street, your newer rival has hung a huge banner: *30% off every pizza.*
Your phone is already buzzing with staff asking what to do. Over the next three months you'll make four calls. Each one builds on the last.

image.label: A rival pizzeria with a big 30% off banner across the street
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 길 양쪽에 피자 가게 두 곳. 오른쪽 가게에 큰 "30% OFF" 현수막, 왼쪽 가게 앞에 앞치마를 두른 주인이 팔짱을 끼고 바라봄. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What a 30% cut would do to you.
cards.callout: You sell about 600 pizzas a week. Matching on all of them drops what's left from **$6,000 to $3,300**. You'd need about 82% more pizzas just to stay even.

cards.title: How do you react today?
body: You don't yet know why the rival cut, how long it will last, or who is switching. Your staff want an answer before the lunch rush.

options.text: Match the 30% today, before customers drift away
options.feedback: You cut $4.50 on all 600 pizzas, including the ones bought by people who were never leaving. That's about $2,700 a week, spent before you know what you're fighting.

options.text: Hold prices for a week and find out who is switching and why
options.feedback: You may lose a few orders, but you buy information. Every next move depends on the rival's reasons and your customers' response.

options.text: Cut 35% to show you won't be pushed around
options.feedback: It costs even more than matching and invites the rival to cut again. You've turned one promotion into a war.

cards.title: Say you waited. Here's what you learned.
body: The banner says *Opening month*. Your weeknight takeout orders fell about 10%, mostly price shoppers. Dine-in and regulars didn't move. The loss: about 60 pizzas, or $600 a week.

image.label: Order chart: weeknight takeout dips, dine-in stays flat
image.brief: 간단한 막대 그래프 두 개. "Weeknight takeout" 막대만 10% 내려가고 "Dine-in"과 "Regulars" 막대는 그대로. 내려간 부분을 주황색으로 강조.

options.text: Match 30% on everything to win back the 10%
options.feedback: You'd spend $2,700 a week to protect $600. If the rival then holds or cuts deeper, you both earn less than before and nobody gains customers.

options.text: Match only where you're losing: $10.50 takeout on weeknights
options.feedback: You defend the slice at risk and keep $10 a pizza everywhere else. The fight stays small and cheap.
You protect your margin, but the rival learns its cut works unopposed, and new takeout habits can stick.

cards.softwareNote: In software, this is a rival slashing its per-seat price. The narrow response is a targeted offer for the users actually churning, such as small teams on monthly plans, instead of repricing every existing customer.

cards.title: Say you matched only weeknight takeout. The rival extends the deal.
body: Your takeout orders are recovering. But the rival's new sign says *30% off until further notice*. You suspect it's testing whether you'll give up.

options.text: Post a public promise at the counter: we match any local takeout price
options.feedback: A public promise is hard to take back, so the rival believes it. Deeper takeout cuts now win it nothing. The cost: you pay the match on those orders, so keep it narrow.

options.text: Stay quiet, keep the weeknight deal and wait it out
options.feedback: Cheap and calm, but the rival can't see your resolve. It may keep cutting to find out.

options.text: Go to 35% off for a month to drive them out
options.feedback: You'd lose money on every pizza, and a rival with deep pockets can outlast you. Both shops bleed.

cards.title: Say you posted the promise. The banner comes down.
body: Two weeks later, the rival quietly returns to $15 a pizza. Your takeout orders are back to normal. You will be neighbors for years.

options.text: Return to $15 too, and leave the match promise posted
options.feedback: You answer peace with peace while the deterrent stays in place. The rival learns cuts get matched and calm gets rewarded.

options.text: Keep the weeknight deal running, just to be safe
options.feedback: It feels safe, but you keep paying $4.50 a pizza for a fight that's over, and customers start treating $10.50 as the real price.

options.text: Cut prices now to steal their customers while they're weak
options.feedback: You restart the war you just ended. In a game played every week, the rival will remember who broke the peace.

cards.title: When this playbook doesn't work.
body: If the rival's costs are truly lower, the cut isn't a promotion. It's its new normal. No clever response wins that game. You need a different position, like better quality or different customers.
A rival backed by investors can also run losses longer than you can. And one move is always off the table: agreeing prices with the rival. In most countries, that's illegal price fixing.

image.label: Two shops with very different cost stacks
image.brief: 두 피자 가게의 비용을 막대로 비교. 한쪽은 비용 막대가 훨씬 짧고 "Lower costs = permanent low price" 라벨. 다른 쪽에 "Change position, not price" 표지판. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: A price cut is a move. Answer it like a game, not a reflex.
body: Each of your four calls used one idea from this unit:
list: **Day 1, read before you react:** game theory basics. Your best move depends on the rival's reasons.
**Week 2, fight narrow:** the prisoner's dilemma. Matching everything leaves both shops worse off.
**Week 5, make it public:** credible commitments. A promise you can't easily undo changes the rival's math.
**Month 3, reward peace:** repeated games. Neighbors who play every week remember.
cards.callout: **Try it today:** write down which of your customers a rival's price cut would actually pull away, and what defending only them would cost.
cards.next: Next · You've finished Game Theory. A new unit starts tomorrow.
